meta.framing: How do experts settle whether a disputed painting is an authentic work by a celebrated master or a later imitation when connoisseurs' stylistic judgments conflict with the findings of pigment analysis, provenance research, and technical imaging?

response:
Disputes of attribution are rarely settled by a single test. Experts settle them by weighing different kinds of evidence against one another and asking which account explains all of them at once. The case of "Portrait of a Scholar" shows how this works. The painting had been attributed to Rembrandt van Rijn by its owner, and connoisseurship appeared to support that claim. Although two senior connoisseurs judged the brushwork of the portrait to be characteristic of Rembrandt's late style, the underdrawing showed none of the compositional changes typical of Rembrandt's working method. Rembrandt habitually revised poses, contours and the placement of hands as he worked. An underdrawing executed without hesitation is therefore more consistent with a copyist reproducing a finished design than with a master inventing one. A confident eye for surface handling cannot, on its own, outweigh that structural silence.

Material analysis sharpened the problem. Pigment analysis detected titanium white in the background of the portrait, and the history of that pigment became central to the dispute. Titanium white pigment became commercially available to artists in the twentieth century. By contrast, titanium white was available to Dutch painters in the 1650s, and this point, unlike the evidence of the underdrawing, tells in favour of the attribution rather than against it. A pigment's date cannot be read off naively. It has to be set against where the pigment occurs on the picture and in which layer of the paint it lies.

Location within the paint structure is decisive here, because a modern pigment confined to one zone may belong to a later intervention rather than to the original campaign of painting. The titanium white in the background indicates that at least one of two things happened to that zone, perhaps both: the original background of the portrait was painted over by a later hand, or the background was extensively retouched by a twentieth-century restorer. That restorer's campaign is in turn the cause of the pigment's twentieth-century availability, since restorers of the period created the demand that brought the pigment into the studio trade. Cross-sections taken at the boundary between figure and ground are the standard means of telling an overpainted original from a wholesale restoration.

The support offers an independent line of evidence. The latest tree ring in the portrait's oak panel dates to 1652; that is, dendrochronology placed the youngest growth ring of the panel in the year 1652. Such a date marks the earliest point at which the tree could have been felled, not the date of the painting. Allowance must also be made for lost sapwood and for seasoning, so a panel of this age remains compatible with both a seventeenth-century master and a later imitator who used old wood. The 1652 date is further confirmed by infrared reflectography, which determines the age of a painting's canvas fibers.

Documentary history must then be reconciled with the physical findings, and here the record forks. Either the portrait was sold at public auction in 1987, or it has never been sold at public auction; the two accounts cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Provenance researchers resolve a conflict of this kind through sale catalogues, auctioneers' day books and dealers' correspondence rather than through an owner's recollection. Weighing the stylistic, structural, material and documentary evidence together, the expert panel concluded that the portrait was a later imitation rather than an authentic work by Rembrandt. That verdict settles the tension between the connoisseurs' reading of the brushwork and the unrevised underdrawing, and the court held that the auction house had wrongly catalogued the portrait as a work by Rembrandt after the panel had reached it. The method, in short, allows no single discipline to overrule the others. Its aim is the account that leaves no finding unexplained.
